headline: Plastic Bottles Are Saving Dolphins From Fishing Nets
meta_description: A Newcastle University researcher discovered that attaching empty bottles to fishing nets helps dolphins detect and avoid them, turning ocean waste into lifesa…
summary_short: Empty plastic bottles attached to fishing nets help dolphins detect invisible gillnets through echolocation, offering a cheap, waste-based solution to a global problem.
body:
Around 1,000 porpoises and hundreds of dolphins die in gillnets across UK waters every year, invisibly ensnared in nylon mesh their echolocation cannot reliably detect. Globally, fishing bycatch remains one of the primary causes of cetacean death. But a researcher at Newcastle University found an elegant solution hiding in ocean waste: empty bottles. Per Berggren's team tested attaching plastic and glass bottles to more than 1,600 fishing nets deployed in Zanzibar, Peru, and Brazil. The science is straightforward. Dolphins navigate and hunt using echolocation—bouncing sound waves off objects to read the echoes. Thin nylon mesh returns no reliable signal. But an air-filled plastic bottle reflects sound differently than water, producing a strong echo dolphins recognize as a warning. Glass bottles fitted with metal bolts create an additional cue: a passive clinking sound as they move with the current.

Results varied by location. In Peru, where nets sit near the surface, the bottles showed no reduction in dolphin bycatch. But Berggren's overall assessment remains positive. "Attaching plastic bottles to fishing nets can reduce dolphin bycatch globally and is something that every fisher can afford," he explains. What makes this approach viable at scale is its simplicity and cost. The bottles attach to existing nets, require no new infrastructure, and can come from waste plastic already spoiling oceans. During trials, no plastic bottles were lost to the sea—they stayed securely fastened throughout. For a problem that has resisted solutions for years, this combination of effectiveness, affordability, and genuine recycling represents something worth serious attention.
quick_facts: 1,000 porpoises and hundreds of dolphins die yearly in UK gillnets alone
Newcastle researcher Per Berggren led trials across Peru, Brazil, and Zanzibar
Empty bottles create sonar echoes that alert dolphins to invisible nylon mesh
Bottles cost almost nothing and use waste plastic from oceans
